source: Newton's Second Law Along an Axis
Add the forces along an axis with signs, then a = ΣF/m.
Students use only the applied force instead of the net force.

Newton's Second Law: F = ma gave $F = ma$. When several forces act, which $F$? The answer is the net force, the sum of all the forces on your free-body diagram, with signs. When that sum is zero, there is no acceleration.
$\Sigma F_x = ma_x$: choose a positive direction, add every force along that axis with its sign, then divide by the mass.

Each force on an object contributes to its acceleration, and forces along a line simply add, with opposite directions subtracting. The object responds to the total, so only the net force sets the acceleration. A large push opposed by large friction can give a small acceleration.
A 2 kg cart pushed with 8 N against 3.9 N of friction accelerates at (8 − 3.9)/2 ≈ 2.0 m/s².
Worked examples
A $5\ \text{kg}$ cart is pulled right with $30\ \text{N}$ and left with $12\ \text{N}$. Find its acceleration (right is $+$).
Two opposite forces
$\Sigma F_x = 30 - 12 = 18\ \text{N}$.
$a = \dfrac{18}{5} = 3.6\ \text{m/s}^2$ to the right.
A $50\ \text{kg}$ model rocket has $800\ \text{N}$ of thrust. Find its acceleration.
Vertical forces
$6.2\ \text{m/s}^2$ up
$a = \dfrac{310}{50} = 6.2\ \text{m/s}^2$ upward.
What horizontal pull gives a $10\ \text{kg}$ box an acceleration of $1.5\ \text{m/s}^2$ against $20\ \text{N}$ of friction?
Finding a force
$F = 35\ \text{N}$: $20\ \text{N}$ to cancel friction and $15\ \text{N}$ to accelerate.

Using only the applied force in $F = ma$ and forgetting friction, weight or other forces. Check: list every arrow on the free-body diagram along the axis of motion, and make sure each one is in your sum with its sign.
